clue.text: Enough clues in fifty puzzles?

indicators.note: puzzles is a verb here: the letters of the words before it are baffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, part of the pool of letters
taken as written, the rest of the pool

explanation.surface: A question about whether fifty crossword puzzles would supply enough clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puzzles' looks like a noun but is the anagram signal acting on the twelve letters of CLUES IN FIFTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an amount that meets what is needed, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Southern song from It's Immaterial

definitions.meaning: a religious folk song of the kind that grew up among enslaved people in the American South
relating to the soul or spirit rather than to the body or physical things

explanation.surface: A song from the Liverpool band It's Immaterial, said to have a Southern flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: It's Immaterial was a 1980s English band, so the surface reads as a band's track; 'from It's' is only link material between the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A gospel-style folk song of the American South carries this name, and the same adjective means relating to the soul rather than bodily matter.

clue.text: Erotic show is loud and a pole and cage is hollow

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
N is the north pole

indicators.note: a hollow word has had its insides scooped out, so only the first and last letters of cage remain

explanation.surface: A seedy burlesque act featuring a dancing pole and a cage with nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: AND and A are used as written; 'is hollow' keeps C and E from 'cage'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a burlesque routine where a dancer teasingly conceals the body behind large feathered fans.

clue.text: For a strong wind, where to put a fireplace

indicators.note: the answer shows the gap where the letter A would go to restore the phrase for stormy weather

parts.note: something meant for a strong wind is for use IN (a) GALE

explanation.surface: Advice on where to site a hearth when a strong wind is blowing.
explanation.walkthrough: Put A into the answer after its G and you get IN GALE, i.e. 'for a strong wind'; so the answer is that phrase with its A taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: An inglenook is a chimney corner, and the older word on its own means a hearth or the fire burning in it.

clue.text: In poor position from mid-point: fifty-fifty on podium

indicators.note: mid- asks for the central letter of the word it is attached to

parts.note: fifty is L in Roman numerals, so two fifties give two Ls
a competitor on the podium has been placed, finishing in the top three

explanation.surface: A competitor ranked badly from halfway, then split evenly for a podium place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mid-point' gives I, the centre of POINT; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something badly sited or positioned unsuitably is described with this hyphenated adjective, an exact synonym phrase.

clue.text: On the ground, it's felt a number had retreated

parts.note: NUM is the abbreviation for number

indicators.note: going back turns the word had round to read from right to left

explanation.surface: Someone senses that a group of people had withdrawn from the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreated' turns HAD into DAH. The definition plays on 'felt' as the verb sensed, when it is the fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A numdah is an Indian felt rug, often embroidered, laid on the floor, so it is felt found on the ground.

clue.text: Thrust forward with no little power

definitions.text: Thrust forward with no little power

indicators.note: with no means doing without, so a letter is taken away from the word before

parts.note: to plunge is to thrust or dive headlong forward
P is the abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A forceful forward thrust delivered with plenty of strength.
explanation.walkthrough: PLUNGE without P gives the answer, and the whole clue also describes a fencer's attacking move made with considerable power.
explanation.definitionFit: A fencer's sudden attacking stride, or any abrupt forward movement, is exactly a forward thrust.

clue.text: 50% of USSR rejected mysterious perestroika

indicators.note: rejected means the letters of USSR are thrown out of the longer word
perestroika means restructuring, so what is left of the other word is rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to be cut down and rearranged
taken as written: the letters removed

explanation.surface: Half of the Soviet Union turned its back on Gorbachev's puzzling reform programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Take U, S, S, R out of MYSTERIOUS to leave MYTEIO, then restructure those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A moiety is one of two parts, a half share, so it equals fifty per cent.

clue.text: The sailors — say 50 — seemingly leave the last one stranded

indicators.note: say signals that the word for the sailors is to be taken by its spoken form

parts.note: the crew is the body of sailors on a ship
written as figures, 50 looks like the letters S and O

indicators.note: the last asks for the final letter of the word leave

explanation.surface: A ship's company abandons its final member on a desert island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives CRU from CREW, '50' resembles SO on the page, and 'the last' of 'leave' gives E. The surface reads 'leave the last one stranded' as one phrase; 'one stranded' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe, Defoe's castaway, is the classic figure marooned alone on an island.

clue.text: A small number? I deny it! Reflecting, it's enough to make you cry

definitions.text: it's enough to make you cry

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirrored, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: NO is the short form of number
no is the word you say to deny something

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a tiny quantity is not theirs, and it brings tears.
explanation.walkthrough: NO + I + NO reads NOINO, and 'Reflecting' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Chopping this bulb releases a compound that stings the eyes and makes people weep.

clue.text: Could be one of 49 or 50 — Boatman's wiser, at last?

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold, and a fiftieth anniversary is a golden one
the setter Boatman speaking of his own things says mine

indicators.note: at last picks out the final letter of the word wiser

explanation.surface: Boatman, reaching fifty, wonders whether he is finally wiser.
explanation.walkthrough: The 49ers were prospectors in the 1849 California gold rush; this is the setter's fiftieth-themed puzzle, so '50' also points at gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A forty-niner was a prospector digging for the precious metal in the California rush of 1849.

clue.text: Islamic State overturns Middle East up in arms

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the two letters are read backwards

parts.note: to be up in arms is to be angry

explanation.surface: A news line about the militant group turning the Middle East into an angry battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Islamic State' looks like the militant group but is the definition: a territory ruled by an emir.
explanation.definitionFit: A territory governed by an emir, a Muslim ruler, is a Muslim state such as one of the UAE members.

clue.text: Refugees from the East taken by 50 states

indicators.note: taken by means captured inside, so one piece is held within the others

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
to aver is to state firmly
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Fifty US states take in people fleeing from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'states' looks like American states but is the verb AVERS; 'taken by' puts E inside L + AVERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Refugees are people who have fled their country, so they are those who depart, a loose synonym.

clue.text: Whether to help, perhaps? Yes, most of the time that's best

parts.note: Y stands for yes on forms that ask for Y or N

indicators.note: most of means one letter is lost from the word for the time

parts.note: asking the hour is asking the time
choice as an adjective means of the best quality

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether they'll help, and told yes, mostly that's the best plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the H of HOUR, leaving OUR; 'perhaps' marks the definition as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Whether to lend a hand is a decision left up to the person asked, the phrase used when handing over a decision.

clue.text: Usually, alcoves in the centre over body of church go up the wall

indicators.note: in a down clue over means written above, so the first piece sits on top of the next
in the centre asks for the middle letter of the seven-letter word alcoves

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
to go up the wall is to become furious

explanation.surface: A church interior where alcoves in the middle rise up the wall above the nave.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre of ALCOVES is O, placed over NAVE and RAGE. 'go up the wall' is British slang for getting very angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken as a whole, typically, and as a rule all mean in the normal run of things.

clue.text: Some 50%, you see, of what you're reading

indicators.note: some means only a part of what follows is used, here a run of letters from the words spelt out

parts.note: written out in words this is fifty percent, and the letters straddling those two words give the answer

explanation.surface: A remark that half of what you're reading is, as you can see, something.
explanation.walkthrough: Spell '50%' as FIFTY PERCENT and the hidden word runs across the join; 'you see' is a conversational link.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed letters, the characters on the page, are collectively called type, which is what the eye reads.

clue.text: He said, "It ain't over 'til it's over, Gary" — or I be mistaken!

definitions.text: He said, "It ain't over 'til it's over

indicators.note: mistaken means got wrong, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, part of the fodder
taken as written, the rest of the fodder

explanation.surface: A famous saying quoted to someone called Gary, unless the speaker is wrong about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine letters of GARY OR I BE rearrange to the name. He was a New York Yankees baseball catcher famous for odd sayings.
explanation.definitionFit: The baseball great is credited with that saying, one of his many celebrated malapropisms and quips.

clue.text: Naughty nature's seized Fifty Shades of Grey

indicators.note: seized means held in a grip, so one letter is gripped inside the jumbled letters
naughty suggests misbehaving, so the letters of the next word are disordered

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A cheeky nature grabs hold of the racy novel Fifty Shades of Grey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' rearranges NATURES to NEUTRAS, and 'seized' puts L inside, after the A. The book title is the misdirection: the definition is colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Greys, beiges and similar colourless tones are called neutrals, so different greys are among them.

clue.text: Here you'll get 50 cobblers

definitions.meaning: on a dartboard, the inner centre circle scores fifty points
British slang for nonsense or rubbish talk

explanation.surface: A sign promising fifty shoe-repairers on site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cobblers' is British slang for nonsense; here it is not shoemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitting the dartboard's inner centre scores fifty, and the same word is slang for rubbish talk.

clue.text: Slate with a step back on top would let air in

indicators.text: with a step back on top
indicators.note: move the first letter one step back in the alphabet, and the answer becomes the word for letting air in

parts.note: to aerate something is to let air into it

explanation.surface: A roof slate that, set with a step at the top, would let a draught in.
explanation.walkthrough: Step the answer's first letter back from B to A and you get AERATE; so the answer is AERATE with its top letter stepped forward to B. 'Slate' here means to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to criticise someone harshly, scold or tell off.

clue.text: Gain backing of European (Irish speaker) for old tenants' association

parts.note: to land a prize is to gain it

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the pieces that follow are read from the end

parts.note: EU, the European Union, stands for European
a Gael is a speaker of Irish Gaelic

explanation.surface: A historical note about an old Irish-speaking European tenants' body gaining support.
explanation.walkthrough: This was the Irish Land League of 1879, which campaigned for the rights of tenant farmers against landlords.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish National Land League was a nineteenth-century organisation campaigning for tenant farmers against landlords.

clue.text: All the same initial odds: below fifty-fifty

indicators.note: in a down clue below means written underneath, so the single letter comes after

parts.note: evens are betting odds where a win pays the same as the stake, a fifty-fifty chance

indicators.note: initial picks the first letter of the word odds

explanation.surface: A betting remark that the opening odds are just under even money.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of 'odds' goes below EVENS. 'Odds' and 'fifty-fifty' both look like the betting picture, but only one is a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean nevertheless or despite that, so they are interchangeable synonyms.

clue.text: State 50 initial hints at Welsh first eleven

indicators.note: initial picks the first letter of each of the three words that follow it

parts.note: A is the first letter of the alphabet, as in grade A
eleven written as figures is two ones, which look like the letters II

explanation.surface: A clue that hints at Welsh selection for the first eleven of a sports team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first eleven' looks like a team; 'first' gives A and 'eleven', as two 1s, gives II.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific island group joined the Union in 1959 as the fiftieth and most recent US state.

clue.text: Anger about current disorder

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: rage is fierce anger
AMP, the ampere, is the unit of electric current

explanation.surface: Anger arising from present-day public unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anger' looks like the definition but is the container; the definition is 'disorder' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A rampage is a spell of violent, uncontrolled behaviour, a kind of riotous disorder.

clue.text: Woman uses 50% of butter substitutes

definitions.meaning: a woman's name, short for Margaret or Marjorie
the informal British short form of margarine, a butter substitute, is about half the full word

explanation.surface: A woman cutting her butter with spreads.
explanation.walkthrough: Marge is the British colloquial clipping of margarine, keeping roughly half the word; 'uses' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a familiar female first name, and the same word is British slang for the spread made instead of dairy fat.

clue.text: The facts: old car maker's failure ultimately having a place in time

parts.note: data are facts and figures
BL is British Leyland, the defunct British car manufacturer

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word failure

explanation.surface: The facts about a defunct carmaker's eventual collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: BL is British Leyland, a British car company of the 1970s and 80s. The surface invites reading its failure as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be assigned a date can be fixed at a point in history, so it occupies a position in time.

clue.text: Fifty-fifty on first of dogs to take rabbit 'ome?

indicators.note: first of asks for the opening letter of the word dogs

parts.note: a rabbit's home is a hutch, and dropping the H in cockney style, as in 'ome, gives the rest

explanation.surface: Dogs sharing evenly in the chase, taking a rabbit home.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'ome signals a dropped H, so HUTCH loses its H. 'Fifty-fifty' as a definition is going Dutch, sharing a cost equally.
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is to split a bill equally, so the word describes an even split of costs.

clue.text: Shrew put spell on a horse, brought back by Tam's leadership

parts.note: a spell is a period of time, such as a school term

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the word for the horse is read in reverse

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

indicators.note: leadership means the leading letter of the word Tam's

explanation.surface: Someone casts a spell on a horse, which a man called Tam then leads back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns NAG into GAN. 'Shrew' is not the animal but a nagging woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a harsh, overbearing woman, which is what a shrew means in the human sense.

clue.text: Camcorders even used in large estates

indicators.note: even asks for the even-numbered letters, the second, fourth and so on, of camcorders

explanation.surface: Video cameras put to use filming big country estates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even' looks like an adverb, as in 'even used', but it picks letters 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural of the land measure loosely stands for extensive grounds or a sizeable landholding.

clue.text: Where cliffs erode, ie St Bees Head

definitions.text: Where cliffs erode, ie St Bees Head

indicators.note: erode means wear away and break up, so the letters that follow are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Cliff erosion described with a real example from England's northwest coast.
explanation.walkthrough: St Bees Head is a sandstone headland on the Cumbrian coast of England. Its words, with IE, rearrange to the answer, and the whole clue describes such a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Cliffs are worn away by waves at the coast, which is exactly next to the ocean, as St Bees Head is.
